newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar passes another milestone, stocks climb.
newsitem.headline: Dollar passes another milestone, stocks climb.

text.p: The dollar passed another milestone against the Japanese yen on Tuesday, prompting a strong rise in Tokyo shares on the view that a lower yen will help exporting companies.
The dollar rose to 126.12 yen, its highest level since February 1993 and up from 124.65 yen in late Tokyo trading on Monday.
Traders said the U.S. currency was pushed up by buying from big Japanese institutional investors eager to take advantage of rising U.S. yields.
The rise, just a day after the dollar chalked up a four-year high of 125 yen, came despite talk of higher Japanese interest rates and possible intervention to slow the U.S. currency's rise.

Kabun Muto, director-general of the Management and Coordination Agency and a senior figure in the ruling Liberal Democratic Party, said that Japan should consider raising interest rates from their current record-low levels.

In addition, Eisuke Sakakibara, the powerful director-general of the Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau, said the Japanese authorities would be ready to intervene in foreign exchange markets if rates veered sharply from economic fundamentals.
"Intervention in the currency markets would be needed to ensure sustainable economic growth if exchange rates were to deviate substantially from economic fundamentals," he said.
The remarks took some speed out of the dollar's rise but traders largely dismissed the news, saying it was not a good time for Japan to intervene in the foreign currency market.
In late Tokyo trading the dollar stood at 126.09 yen, a shade off its high, compared with a late U.S. level on Monday of around 125.62 yen.
The weakening yen helped boost shares of big exporting companies since it increases the value of their earnings from abroad, but some market sectors remained weak.
The 225-share Nikkei average rose 306.03 points, or 1.73 percent, to end at 18,021.70. Its June futures finished 390 points higher at 18,040.

"A small handful of shares supported by a weakening yen boosted the indices, but securities, construction and most banks were still pitifully weak and declining issues outnumbered the gainers," said Akihiro Naemura, Okasan Securities general manager.
On the first section of the Tokyo Stock Exchange, losing issues outnumbered gainers 646 to 497, while 99 issues were unchanged. Turnover was some 477 million shares, up from 410 million on Monday.
